Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_011k5qHXZ4d4ZCkrxtQvHM9G","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. Memory\n63\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n64\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n65\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n66\t\n67\t### 7. Orchestration\n68\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n69\t- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n70\t  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n71\t\n72\t### 8. Routing\n73\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n74\t- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n75\t  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n76\t\n77\t### 9. Feedback\n78\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n79\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n80\t- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n81\t  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n82\t  poisoning path.)\n83\t\n84\t## Notes\n85\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n86\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n87\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n88\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n89\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n90\t  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n91\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"4e15b83e-4615-4f36-977c-e7ba34354abc","uuid":"47e8dcf3-a75c-4998-b247-2dbd43b9a3d2","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:25:01.526Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\ai-systems.md","content":"# AI / agentic layer — detail\n\nLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). They add risk/security and organizational\n  dependencies, such as a business associate agreement before patient data reaches a new\n  vendor, and the skeleton still runs in production on a designated test record.\n","numLines":118,"startLine":1,"totalLines":118}}}

Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A service that scores every card authorization inline, using streamed per-card features and an ML model on top of rules. The decision has to fit inside the auth path's time slice, and it has to be right.\n- **Worst failure:** The scorer causes legitimate customers to be declined in bulk, through a bad model, a bad threshold push, or a timeout that the auth path turns into declines. A wrong decline cannot be taken back. The second worst is card numbers (PANs) leaking out of the PCI cardholder-data environment (CDE) into features, logs or training data. Those are guarded by V5 and V4.\n\n**Starting assumptions (the plan's shape depends on them):** We are a card issuer, or an issuer-processor. There is an existing auth platform, an existing rules engine that also serves as the fallback, a token vault or HSM, case management, and Kafka. If we are actually an acquirer, PSP or merchant, the integration point becomes a pre-auth API and the labels come from chargebacks through the acquirer. The phase order stays the same. If we are a processor serving many issuers, tenant isolation becomes an extra R3 row and a gate before Phase 3.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency (scorer, measured at the caller) | p99 ≤ 50 ms; hard timeout 75 ms, then fall back to the existing rules | ASSUMPTION: a typical inline fraud slice for an issuer-processor. The auth platform owner confirms the real slice in Phase 0. | V0 records the floor; V2 |\n| Throughput | Design target 2× peak authorizations per second | BASELINE: peak TPS over the last 12 months, including the seasonal peak, taken from auth logs in Phase 0. The 2× headroom is an ASSUMPTION (seasonal growth plus attack bursts). | V2 |\n| Availability | No drop in auth-path success rate or latency compared with today; scorer fallback rate ≤ 0.1% of transactions per day | BASELINE (auth path, Phase 0) / ASSUMPTION (above that rate, fraud protection is effectively off too often) | V5; fallback-rate SLO from Phase 3 |\n| Fraud efficacy | — | UNKNOWN: the acceptable false-decline rate and the value of fraud caught per legitimate decline. The head of fraud risk supplies these in Phase 1; V7 needs them. | V1, V7 |\n| Label maturity | Most confirmed fraud is reported within 90 days | ASSUMPTION: based on typical claim and chargeback windows. The real maturity curve is measured from history in Phase 2. | Phase 2 exit check |\n| RPO / RTO | Decision log RPO ≤ 1 min, reconciled against the auth platform log. Online feature store RTO ≤ 1 h, rebuilt from the event log; the scorer degrades or falls back while it rebuilds. | ASSUMPTION: every decision must be reconstructable for disputes and model review | Phase 3 rebuild drill |\n| Storage / retention | — | UNKNOWN: the record-retention policy (compliance), needed before the Phase 2 backfill. Training needs at least 13 months for seasonality (ASSUMPTION). | Phase 2 |\n| Run cost against fraud loss avoided | — | UNKNOWN: finance supplies the cost ceiling and how avoided losses are valued, by Phase 2 | V1 |\n| Operational complexity | One scoring service, one stream job, one online store, one offline training pipeline. On-call is 24/7, but a scorer outage is a degraded state (fallback), not an outage. | ASSUMPTION: a single owning team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\n**Missing inputs:**\n- Our role (issuer, acquirer or merchant).\n- The real latency slice in the auth path.\n- What the existing fraud stack contains (rules engine, network scores such as Visa VAA or Mastercard Decision Intelligence, case management).\n- How many months of labeled history exist.\n- The PCI DSS scope boundary and who our QSA is.\n- The model-risk policy (for example SR 11-7 in the US).\n- The jurisdiction. In the EU, GDPR Art. 22 applies to automated decisions, and PSD2 TRA fraud-rate reporting applies if exemptions are used. Both add organizational dependencies before Phase 5.\n\n## 2. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The request:** A real authorization on an internal test card at a real merchant (a small card-not-present purchase). The scorer returns a stub score and a reason code. The auth platform logs that response and ignores it. The existing rules make the actual decision.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Card network\n  2. Auth platform hook (tokenizes the card number, checks the flag and allow-list)\n  3. Scorer over mTLS (schema validation, increments one velocity counter in the online store, stub rules and model)\n  4. Response back to the auth platform\n  5. Decision event to Kafka\n  6. Decision log store\n  7. Dashboard\n- **Day zero:**\n  - Deployed through CI/CD from IaC with pinned images.\n  - Traces use the auth correlation ID and the token, never the PAN. Tokenization hardened at the hook, plus PAN scanners on every topic, log and store (V4 continues).\n    3. Fail-safe path, tested against a stub that declines everything, on test cards (V5):\n       - hard timeout falling back to the existing rules\n       - kill switch\n       - circuit breaker on decline rate, comparing treatment with control\n       - malformed-response handling\n    4. Record the confirmed latency slice in V2.\n  - Rollback: schema changes are expand/contract only; the hook can be switched off with a flag.\n  - Exit check: V5 passes; contract tests pass in CI; the UNKNOWN inputs have numbers.\n\n- **Phase 2: History, labels, offline model**\n  - Unlocks: the build-vs-buy decision and the design of the streaming platform.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, V4, data-access approval.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Label pipeline joining claims and chargebacks to transactions, plus the 200-sample label audit.\n    3. Measure the label-maturity curve.\n    4. Score the existing rules on the same history to get their baseline.\n    5. Train a gradient-boosted model using only features that can be computed online within the latency slice (V1).\n    6. The model served in-process from a signed registry artifact.\n    4. Every authorization mirrored async to the scorer. Shadow only; the auth path does not wait for it.\n    5. Load test (V2) and parity check (V3).\n    6. Rebuild-the-store drill and DR drill.\n  - Rollback: stop the mirror; the online store is disposable and rebuilt from the log.\n  - Exit check: V2 and V3 pass; the store rebuild meets the RTO.\n\n- **Phase 4: Analyst advisory**\n  - Unlocks: the first human use of scores, and labels within days instead of the 90-day maturity window.\n  - Depends on: V3, V5, V6.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Log reason codes.\n  - Rollback: switch off the queue feed; the existing rules' alerts carry on.\n  - Exit check: the precision of score-driven alerts, as judged by analysts, is no worse than the existing rules' alerts over 2 weeks; no regression in auth latency.\n\n- **Phase 5: Decision canary, then widen**\n  - Unlocks: model-driven declines for everyone.\n  - Depends on: V5, V6, plus the EU legal review if it applies.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The request:** A real authorization on an internal test card at a real merchant (a small card-not-present purchase). The scorer returns a stub score and a reason code. The auth platform logs that response and ignores it. The existing rules make the actual decision.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Card network\n  2. Auth platform hook (tokenizes the card number, checks the flag and allow-list)\n  3. Scorer over mTLS (schema validation, increments one velocity counter in the online store, stub rules and model)\n  4. Response back to the auth platform\n  5. Decision event to Kafka\n  6. Decision log store\n  7. Dashboard\n- **Day zero:**\n  - Deployed through CI/CD from IaC with pinned images.\n  - Traces use the auth correlation ID and the token, never the PAN. Telemetry is classified as cardholder-adjacent and access to it is restricted.\n  - Alerts fire on scorer errors and latency, and on a change in auth latency.\n  - One rollback is rehearsed: redeploy the previous version, then switch the flag off.\n- **Discovery and baselines, also in Phase 0:** Find everything that consumes the existing rules' output. Through the auth platform's own change process, baseline auth p99, peak TPS, the existing rules' decline rate, fraud losses in basis points, and the false-positive rate.\n- **Lead-time items started in Phase 0:** QSA engagement, model-risk validator time, data-access approval, and the efficacy targets from fraud risk.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only allow-listed internal test-card tokens, behind a flag. The response cannot change any decision; it is a dry run.\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- The test authorization succeeds with one trace across every tier.\n- A deploy and a rollback succeed through the pipeline.\n- Killing the scorer fires an alert, and the auth path's outcome and latency do not change.\n- Auth latency with and without the hook, and scorer p99 at near-zero load, are recorded as baselines.\n\n## 5. Phases\n- **Phase 1: Contracts and safety rails**\n  - Unlocks: real data leaving the CDE; any later use of a score.\n  - Depends on: V0.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Canonical event schema in the registry, with contract tests on real auth message samples.\n    2. Tokenization hardened at the hook, plus PAN scanners on every topic, log and store (V4 continues).\n    3. Fail-safe path, tested against a stub that declines everything, on test cards (V5):\n       - hard timeout falling back to the existing rules\n       - kill switch\n       - circuit breaker on decline rate, comparing treatment with control\n       - malformed-response handling\n    4. Get the efficacy and cost inputs (UNKNOWN in §1) from the head of fraud risk and from finance.\n    5. Record the confirmed latency slice in V2.\n  - Rollback: schema changes are expand/contract only; the hook can be switched off with a flag.\n  - Exit check: V5 passes; contract tests pass in CI; the UNKNOWN inputs have numbers.\n\n- **Phase 2: History, labels, offline model**\n  - Unlocks: the build-vs-buy decision and the design of the streaming platform.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, V4, data-access approval.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Backfill at least 13 months of tokenized auth history into the offline lake, under the retention policy.\n    2. Label pipeline joining claims and chargebacks to transactions, plus the 200-sample label audit.\n    3. Measure the label-maturity curve.\n    4. Score the existing rules on the same history to get their baseline.\n    5. Train a gradient-boosted model using only features that can be computed online within the latency slice (V1).\n    6. Start model documentation for V6.\n  - Rollback: everything is offline; derived datasets are deleted under the retention policy.\n  - Exit check: V1 passes; the label audit passes.\n\n- **Phase 3: Streaming features and full-traffic shadow**\n  - Unlocks: trustworthy online scores.\n  - Depends on: V1, V4.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Single feature definitions that compile to both the Flink job and the offline batch.\n    2. Online store keyed by token, with inline velocity counters.\n    3. The model served in-process from a signed registry artifact.\n    4. Every authorization mirrored async to the scorer. Shadow only; the auth path does not wait for it.\n    5. Load test (V2) and parity check (V3).\n    6. Rebuild-the-store drill and DR drill.\n  - Rollback: stop the mirror; the online store is disposable and rebuilt from the log.\n  - Exit check: V2 and V3 pass; the store rebuild meets the RTO.\n\n- **Phase 4: Analyst advisory**\n  - Unlocks: the first human use of scores, and labels within days instead of the 90-day maturity window.\n  - Depends on: V3, V5, V6.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Switch to the inline call (hard timeout) for all traffic, with the score logged but not used to decide.\n    2. Send high scores to the case-management queue; analysts decide.\n    3. Log reason codes.\n  - Rollback: switch off the queue feed; the existing rules' alerts carry on.\n  - Exit check: the precision of score-driven alerts, as judged by analysts, is no worse than the existing rules' alerts over 2 weeks; no regression in auth latency.\n\n- **Phase 5: Decision canary, then widen**\n  - Unlocks: model-driven declines for everyone.\n  - Depends on: V5, V6, plus the EU legal review if it applies.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Hashed card cohorts at 1%, then 5%, 25% and 100%, each with a matched control on the existing rules only.\n    2. Threshold changes are versioned config shipped through the pipeline, approved by two people.\n    3. V7 must pass at each step before widening.\n  - Rollback: the per-cohort kill switch puts that cohort on rules only (tested in V5). There is no point of no return because the existing rules are kept. Wrong declines cannot be undone, which is why V5 and V7 come before each step.\n  - Exit check: V7 passes at 100%; the breaker has not tripped for 30 days.\n\n- **Phase 6: Feedback and model lifecycle**\n  - Unlocks: sustained performance as fraud patterns shift.\n  - Depends on: Phase 5.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Monthly retraining on matured labels.\n    2. Champion/challenger: the challenger runs in shadow before promotion.\n    3. Drift alerts on feature distributions (PSI).\n    4. Label corrections reviewed by fraud ops; first-party claims excluded.\n    5. Each promotion goes through model-risk review as in V6.\n  - Rollback: roll the registry back to the previous champion.\n  - Exit check: a challenger beats the champion out-of-time and in shadow before it is promoted, with no segment getting worse.\n\n## 6. Deliberately deferred\n- **Active-active multi-region scoring:** pulled forward if the DR drill shows fallback-mode losses that fraud risk will not accept.\n- **Async graph or ring detection** (mule networks, compromised merchants): pulled forward when fraud ops reports patterns that per-card features miss.\n- **Separate models per segment** (card-present vs card-not-present) with routing: pulled forward when one segment trails the overall model by more than the agreed margin.\n- **3DS step-up as a softer action than decline:** pulled forward when the issuer's 3DS access control server can be integrated.\n- **Exploration traffic** (approving a small sample of flagged transactions to get unbiased labels): only with explicit approval from fraud risk, and once selection bias is measured to distort retraining.\n- **Sequence or deep-learning models:** pulled forward when the gradient-boosted model plateaus across two retraining cycles.\n- **Decommissioning the existing rules:** not in this plan; they are the fallback. Pulled forward only if their run cost becomes significant.
